title: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha
author: Aharon Hyman

paragraphs: The early commentators disagree about the identity of Korcha, the father of this great tanna. Rashi, in Shevuot 6a and Bekhorot 58a, understands Ben Azzai's statement, “All the sages of Israel are like garlic peel before me, except for this bald man,” as referring to Rabbi Akiva. On that reading, the Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha named throughout the Talmud is Rabbi Akiva's son. Rabbenu Gershom explains it likewise in Bekhorot, as does Rashbam in Pesachim 112a, and Ri in Tosafot to Bava Batra 113a, s.v. u-matu. All cite Bekhorot. Our Talmud texts do not expressly say that Ben Azzai meant Rabbi Akiva. Tosafot to Bekhorot 58a, s.v. chutz, cite Rabbenu Nissim's view that the bald man was Rabbi Elazar ben Azariah, who was said to be bald. Hyman did not find this in his Yerushalmi or in the recently printed Yerushalmi Bekhorot. The Arukh, under kereach, gives Ben Azzai's words and identifies the man as Rabbi Akiva bar Yosef. Hyman infers that this was the Arukh's Talmud reading.[^1][^2]

The Tosafists, in Shabbat 150a, Pesachim 112a, Bava Batra 113a, and Bekhorot 58a, rejected the identification. If Ben Azzai once called Rabbi Akiva bald, why would his son consistently be called ben Korcha instead of ben Rabbi Akiva? They also cite Megillah 28a, where Rabbi asked Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha for a blessing and was told, “May you reach half my years.” If he was Rabbi Akiva's son, Rabbi was born when Rabbi Akiva died. Even if Rabbi Yehoshua was born in the first year after Akiva married Kalba Savua's daughter, he would have been at most 140 then. He would hardly bless Rabbi with less than seventy years, yet Rabbi was already sixty. What, then, was the blessing? Rabbenu Tam therefore says in Shabbat and Bava Batra that Korcha was a person's name, like Korach.

Seder HaDorot objects that people do not name children after the wicked. Hyman sees no difficulty. Korach's sons are regularly named in Psalms in the heading “A maskil of the sons of Korach.” He also suggests that the name may have been changed from Korach to Korcha for that very reason.

Hyman refers back to his entry on Rabbi Akiva for his response to Rabbenu Tam's argument from Megillah. Avot deRabbi Natan, at the beginning of chapter 6, describes Akiva as already having a son when he married Kalba Savua's daughter. On Hyman's reconstruction Rabbi Yehoshua would thus have been about 160 when he blessed Rabbi, wishing him eighty years. Hyman finds some evidence against the identification in Sanhedrin 110b. On “those who make a covenant with Me over a sacrifice,” Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha says, “These are Rabbi Akiva and his colleagues.” Hyman argues that if Akiva were his father he would have said, “my father and teacher and his colleagues.”[^3]

Who were his teachers? In Tosefta Negaim 7:3 and Kelim Bava Batra chapter 2 he speaks in the name of Rabbi Elazar ben Azariah. In Yerushalmi Kilayim 4:2, Rabbi Yochanan relates that Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha visited Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri at Nagnigar. The latter showed him a field and described a Sabbath partition by comparison. Hyman takes this as some indication that he received teaching from him. Eruvin 11b names Rabbi Yehoshua ben Hananiah as the visitor. Hyman proposes a scribal error and prefers the Yerushalmi's reading, which he also reports in Yerushalmi Eruvin chapter 1, at the beginning of Yerushalmi Sukkah, and in Rabbenu Hananel's text.[^4]

Hyman counts four mentions in the Mishnah, all tending toward aggadah. In Berakhot 2:2 he explains why Shema precedes Ve-haya. In Rosh Hashanah 4:4 he reports another enactment of Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai. In Nedarim 3:11 he declares the greatness of circumcision. In Sanhedrin 7:5 he says that throughout the proceedings the witnesses use a substitute name.

The Talmud also preserves legal teachings from him in baraitot. In Ketubot 26b, testimony can be combined even when given separately. In Kiddushin 41b, a person's agent acts as the person himself. In Bava Metzia 104a, he interprets ordinary contractual language so that a lender cannot take a pledge worth more than the debt. In Avodah Zarah 6b, one may not collect a debt recorded in a written instrument from them, but may collect an oral loan. At 7a, one may ask another person whether he will be available that evening. In a matter of Torah law one follows the stricter opinion, and in a rabbinic matter the more lenient opinion. In Chullin 50b, he identifies the inner rumen as the sanya de-veivei.

His aggadic teachings. In Berakhot 7a, God tells Moses that when He wished to reveal Himself, Moses did not wish it, and now that Moses wishes it, He does not. In Megillah 13a, Esther had a greenish complexion. In 15a, Malachi is Ezra. In 15b he asks why Esther invited Haman. In Sanhedrin 6b he derives from “You shall not be intimidated by anyone” that a pupil sitting before his teacher must speak up if he sees a point in favor of the poor litigant and against the rich one. In 7a he says it is a mitzvah to seek a compromise. In 99a, learning Torah without reviewing it is like sowing without reaping. In 21a he says that Tamar established a great safeguard by what she did then. In 94a, because Pharaoh himself blasphemed, God Himself exacted punishment from him.

The amoraim also transmitted his teachings. Hyman cites Rabbi Chiyya bar Avin in Yoma 39b, Megillah 14a, Gittin 57b, and Bava Batra 91b. Bava Kamma 38b names Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba in the teaching that one should always be early to perform a mitzvah. Hyman proposes reading Rabbi Chiyya bar Avin. In Ketubot 68a, Rabbi Chiyya bar Rav of Difti teaches in Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha's name that turning a blind eye to charity is like worshipping idols. Hyman also lists aggadic appearances in Megillah 25b, Moed Katan 23a, Bava Batra 15b, Sanhedrin 19b and 108a, Zevachim 102a and 115b, and Menachot 56b.

Disputes with sectarians. Hyman says he often disputed with Sadducees. In Shabbat 152a a eunuch asks him how far it is to Baldtown. He replies by asking how far it is to Eunuchtown. Seeing that the rabbi wears no shoes, the man says that one who rides a horse is a king, one on a donkey a free man, and one with shoes on his feet a human being, and so on. The rabbi replies, “Eunuch, eunuch, you said three things and heard three things. A beard is the glory of the face, a wife the joy of the heart, and children the inheritance of the Lord. Blessed is God who has spared you all of them.”[^5]

In Bereshit Rabbah 13:6 a gentile asks when both peoples rejoice together, and he answers, “When rain falls.” At the end of chapter 27, a sectarian asks how God can foresee the future if Scripture says He was grieved at heart. Rabbi Yehoshua answers that joy belongs to the time of joy. In Shemot Rabbah 2:5 a gentile asks why God spoke to Moses out of the bush. The answer is that no place is empty of the Divine Presence. In Vayikra Rabbah 4:6, Rabbi Elaza relates that a gentile challenged him from the Torah's instruction to follow the majority. Gentiles outnumber Israel, yet Israel does not join in their worship. The rabbi replies that they are divided into many sects with different objects of worship, and shows the man that his own sons each pray to a different god. On this reckoning, Hyman concludes, Israel is the majority.

His colleagues. In Avodah Zarah 7b he and Rabbi Shimon both say that penitents are accepted either way, citing “Return, wayward children.” Hyman takes the attribution in Midrash Tehillim 78:9 to Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai to be a scribal error.

He disagrees with Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel in Nedarim 31b. In old age he sat with Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, with Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Shimon, after his father's death, and Rabbi sitting before them, as in Bava Metzia 84b. In Bava Batra 113a Rabbi Yannai cites Rabbi, and the teaching is also transmitted in Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha's name. In Midrash Tehillim 1:8, Rabbi expresses surprise at how Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha taught him. At 92:3 Rabbi Yose son of Rabbi Yehudah and Rabbi went to ask him a question. At the beginning of Megillah Rabbi Yose son of Rabbi Yehudah raises an objection. In Bava Metzia 83b, when Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Shimon was appointed to catch thieves, Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha sent him the message, “Vinegar son of wine, how long will you hand over the people of our God to be killed?” He answered, “I am clearing thorns from the vineyard.” The rabbi replied, “Let the owner of the vineyard come and clear his thorns.”

Hyman finds that he had pupils in Vayikra Rabbah 4:6. Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachman speaks in his name in Vayikra Rabbah 1:3 and in Kohelet Rabbah on “Vanity of vanities.” Rabbi Berechyah speaks in his name in Tanchuma, Chukkat 21, and Hyman also cites Pesikta deRav Kahana 38.

He lived to a great age, as told in Megillah 28a. Rabbi asked how he had lived so long. “Do you begrudge me my life?” he replied. Rabbi said, “It is Torah, and I need to learn.” He answered that he had never looked at the likeness of a wicked person. As he was dying, Rabbi asked him for a blessing. He wished Rabbi half his years. Rabbi asked why not all of them. “Will those who come after you tend cattle?” he replied. Sefer Yuchasin says Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha lived twice as long as Rabbi, connecting this with “You shall decree a thing, and it shall be established for you.” Seder HaDorot objects that he might have lived many years after the blessing. Hyman replies that the passage expressly places the blessing at his death. Rabbi Chaim Vital's writings report in the name of the Ari that there were two sages named Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha. Hyman closes, “If this is a received tradition, we accept it.”[^6]

notes.text: The Hebrew was transcribed against Hyman’s printed volume II, pp. 648–650, corresponding to scan pages 231–233. The machine transcription is retained in the source record. Printed references and Hyman’s own proposed readings are preserved.

Bekhorot 58a itself leaves “this bald man” unnamed. Rashi on Shevuot 6a expressly identifies Yehoshua son of Rabbi Akiva with Yehoshua ben Korcha. Tosafot on Bekhorot 58a report Rabbenu Nissim’s identification of the bald man as Rabbi Elazar ben Azariah and Rabbenu Tam’s reading of Korcha as a personal name. The remark and the question of paternity are distinct.

Megillah 28a gives a blessing of half his years at his death. It supplies no ages. The numbers are part of the chronological arguments reported by Hyman. Sanhedrin 110b names Rabbi Akiva and his colleagues, from which Hyman draws his qualified inference about paternity.

The consulted Yerushalmi Kilayim 4:2 explicitly names Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha. The consulted Bavli Eruvin 11b names Rabbi Yehoshua without a patronymic in this passage. Hyman reports the ben Hananiah reading and proposes a correction. The textual difference does not by itself establish a teacher–pupil relationship.
Hyman describes the dispute as one with Sadducees, while the consulted Shabbat 152a names the interlocutor with the Aramaic term goza’ah. The exchange plays on the participants’ physical traits.

Megillah 28a reports the deathbed blessing. Hyman’s report of two sages of the same name is attributed to Rabbi Chaim Vital in the Ari’s name. This article retains the different identifications without combining or dividing the historical persons.
